title: Python Concurrency Models Compared
summary: Compares Python's concurrency models: threads under the GIL, free-threaded 3.13+, multiprocessing, asyncio, and structured concurrency with trio and anyio. Covers how to pick one by workload, how to mix models safely, shared-state pitfalls, and how to benchmark to see whether concurrency helps.

chapters.title: Concurrency vs Parallelism: The Fundamentals
points: Concurrency means managing several tasks whose lifetimes overlap. Parallelism means executing several tasks at the same instant on multiple cores
I/O-bound work spends most of its time waiting on network, disk or a DB. CPU-bound work spends it computing in the interpreter
Preemptive multitasking (threads): the OS or interpreter can switch tasks at any bytecode boundary, without the code asking
Cooperative multitasking (asyncio, trio): a task gives up control only at an explicit await point
Python's four main models are threading, multiprocessing, asyncio (coroutines) and native extensions that release the GIL
Unit cost differs a lot: a coroutine is a small heap object, a thread has an OS stack, and a process is a whole interpreter with its own memory
concurrent.futures gives one Executor API (submit, map, Future.result) for both threads and processes
A Future is a placeholder for a result that isn't ready yet. concurrent.futures.Future is a different class from asyncio.Future
Blocking call vs non-blocking call: a blocking call holds up only its own thread, but in asyncio it holds up the whole event loop
Amdahl's law: speedup ≤ 1 / (serial_fraction + parallel_fraction/N), so the serial part caps the gain
Rule of thumb: waiting is solved by concurrency, and computing is solved by parallelism

chapters.title: Threading and the GIL
points: The GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) is a mutex in CPython: only one thread runs Python bytecode at a time
The GIL exists to protect reference counts and interpreter internals cheaply, and it keeps C extensions simple
Switch interval: a thread waiting for the GIL asks the running thread to release it after sys.getswitchinterval() (default 0.005 s)
The GIL is released during blocking I/O (socket recv, file read), time.sleep, and select/poll
C extensions can release the GIL during heavy work, e.g. NumPy operations, hashlib on large buffers, zlib compression
So threads do speed up I/O-bound code, but pure-Python CPU-bound code gets no speedup and can even get slower from contention
threading.Thread(target=f, args=(x,)).start() then .join(). daemon=True threads are killed abruptly when the interpreter exits
ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n) reuses threads. Its default max_workers is min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4)
Example: executor.map(fetch, urls) downloads 100 URLs about N× faster than a serial loop, because the threads overlap their network waits
Exceptions in a bare Thread don't reach the caller. They go to threading.excepthook, while Future.result() re-raises them
Threads can't be killed from outside. Stop them cooperatively with a threading.Event flag that the thread checks
Thread stacks reserve virtual memory (often 8 MB on Linux), so thousands of threads are feasible but not free

chapters.title: Free-Threaded Python (3.13+)
points: PEP 703 added an optional build with the GIL removed: python3.13t, the 't' suffix, built with --disable-gil
It was experimental in 3.13. PEP 779 made it officially supported (no longer experimental) in 3.14, but it is still not the default build
Check at runtime with sys._is_gil_enabled(). Force the GIL back on with PYTHON_GIL=1 or -X gil=1
How it stays safe without the GIL: biased reference counting (cheap for the owning thread), immortal objects, and the mimalloc allocator
Built-in containers like dict and list use per-object locks (critical sections), so single operations don't corrupt them
Pure-Python CPU-bound threads can now run on multiple cores in parallel, which gives near-linear speedup for independent work
Single-threaded code runs slower: about 40% in 3.13 (specializing interpreter disabled), cut to roughly 5-10% in 3.14
Importing a C extension that doesn't declare Py_mod_gil support re-enables the GIL and emits a warning
Removing the GIL exposes latent races: a compound operation like `d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1` still needs a Lock
Before adopting it, check that your dependencies ship cp313t/cp314t wheels

chapters.title: multiprocessing and ProcessPoolExecutor
points: Each worker process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, which gives true CPU parallelism even on GIL builds
Start methods: fork (copies the parent; fast, but unsafe with threads), spawn (fresh interpreter; slow, safe) and forkserver
Default start method by platform: spawn on Windows and on macOS since 3.8, forkserver on Linux since 3.14 (fork before that)
Forking a process that has threads can deadlock on inherited locks. Since 3.12 Python emits a DeprecationWarning for it
The if __name__ == '__main__': guard is required with spawn. Without it, each child re-imports the main module and spawns more workers
Arguments and results are pickled across the process boundary, so lambdas, local functions and open sockets can't be sent
ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=os.cpu_count()) with submit/map and as_completed() handles results in the order they finish
chunksize in map() batches items per IPC round trip and is essential when there are many tiny tasks
max_tasks_per_child (3.11+) recycles workers to contain memory leaks
A worker crash (segfault, OOM kill) raises BrokenProcessPool, and the pool must be recreated
multiprocessing.shared_memory (3.8+) shares raw buffers such as NumPy arrays without pickling
Cost: process startup takes tens of ms plus per-call serialization, so each task should do far more work than that overhead

chapters.title: asyncio: Event Loop and Coroutines
points: `async def` defines a coroutine function. Calling it returns a coroutine object, and nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled
The event loop runs one thread, uses OS readiness APIs (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), and resumes coroutines whose I/O is ready
asyncio.run(main()) creates the loop, runs it, and closes it. It is the single entry point for a program
asyncio.create_task(coro) schedules the coroutine to run concurrently. `await coro` alone runs it sequentially
asyncio.gather(*aws) runs awaitables concurrently. By default the first exception propagates but the sibling tasks keep running
asyncio.TaskGroup (3.11+) is structured: if one task fails, the others are cancelled and an ExceptionGroup is raised
`async with asyncio.timeout(5):` (3.11+) sets a deadline. Prefer it to wrapping calls in wait_for
Cancellation injects CancelledError at an await point. Re-raise it after cleanup and never swallow it
Keep a reference to every task you create. The loop holds only weak references, so an unreferenced task can be garbage-collected mid-run
asyncio.Semaphore(n) caps in-flight requests, e.g. 10k URLs with at most 100 open at once
A blocking call such as time.sleep, requests.get or a heavy loop freezes every coroutine. Debug mode (PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1) logs callbacks slower than 100 ms
It scales to tens of thousands of sockets because each waiting coroutine costs only a few KB, not an OS thread

chapters.title: Structured Concurrency: trio and anyio
points: Structured concurrency: every task lives inside a lexical scope that can't exit until all of its child tasks finish
trio nursery: `async with trio.open_nursery() as n: n.start_soon(f)`. The block waits for all its children
If a child fails, its siblings are cancelled and the errors surface together as an ExceptionGroup, handled with except* (3.11+)
Cancel scopes: trio.move_on_after(5) silently stops the block, while fail_after(5) raises TooSlowError
Cancellation is level-triggered: every checkpoint inside a cancelled scope keeps raising Cancelled, so cleanup can't accidentally continue
Checkpoints are the await points where trio may switch or cancel. trio.sleep(0) yields explicitly
anyio is an API that runs on either the asyncio or the trio backend, selected via anyio.run(main, backend='trio')
anyio.create_task_group() gives nursery semantics on top of plain asyncio
anyio.CapacityLimiter bounds concurrency, and anyio.to_thread.run_sync offloads blocking calls
Compared with plain asyncio: no orphaned tasks, no silently lost exceptions, and timeouts that nest correctly
asyncio.TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout adopted these ideas, but create_task outside a group still escapes the structure

chapters.title: Mixing Models Safely
points: await asyncio.to_thread(fn, *args) (3.9+) runs a blocking function in the default thread pool and copies contextvars
loop.run_in_executor(executor, fn, *args) takes only positional args, so use functools.partial for kwargs
CPU-bound work from async code: run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), fn, x) keeps the event loop responsive
asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, loop) submits a coroutine from another thread and returns a concurrent.futures.Future
loop.call_soon_threadsafe(cb) is the only safe way for another thread to touch the loop. A plain call_soon from another thread is a bug
Never call asyncio.run() inside a running loop: it raises RuntimeError. Await the coroutine instead
Calling future.result() on the loop's own thread for a future scheduled on that loop deadlocks, because the loop can't progress
asyncio primitives (Lock, Queue, Event) are not thread-safe. Use queue.Queue or janus to bridge between threads and the loop
anyio.from_thread.run(async_fn) lets a worker thread call back into the event loop
A long-lived sync app can run the loop in a background thread and call run_coroutine_threadsafe(...).result(timeout) from sync code
The default executor is shared. Set loop.set_default_executor(...) or use a dedicated pool so slow calls don't starve it

chapters.title: Shared-State Pitfalls
points: counter += 1 is not atomic: it compiles to load, add and store bytecodes, so a thread switch in between loses updates
The GIL protects the interpreter, not your invariants. Check-then-act code still races, with or without the GIL
`with lock:` (threading.Lock) guarantees release on exceptions. RLock lets the same thread re-acquire it
Deadlock: two locks acquired in opposite orders. Fix it with a global lock ordering or a single coarser lock
Prefer message passing: queue.Queue producer/consumer avoids most explicit locks
asyncio races happen across await points: `if key not in cache: cache[key] = await fetch()` can fetch twice
In multiprocessing, a global mutated in a child is invisible to the parent because each process has separate memory
Manager().dict() proxies are shared, but every access is an IPC round trip and orders of magnitude slower
multiprocessing.Value and Array need `with v.get_lock():` for read-modify-write updates
threading.local holds per-thread state. contextvars.ContextVar holds per-task state that is correct under asyncio
Free-threaded builds make rare races frequent. Stress-test with many threads and a small sys.setswitchinterval

chapters.title: Choosing by Workload, Benchmarks, and When Concurrency Doesn't Help
points: Many sockets with async libraries (aiohttp, asyncpg) → asyncio or anyio
Moderate I/O through blocking libraries (requests, boto3, DB drivers) → ThreadPoolExecutor
Pure-Python CPU work → ProcessPoolExecutor, or threads on a free-threaded build
Numeric CPU work → vectorize with NumPy or Numba first. Threads work because these libraries release the GIL
Typical benchmark: CPU-bound fib on 4 cores takes about serial time with threads under the GIL and about serial/4 with processes
I/O benchmark: 100 requests at 100 ms each take ~10 s serially and ~0.1-0.3 s with threads or asyncio
Measure with time.perf_counter() or pyperf, with warm-up and repeats. Never trust a single time.time() run
Profile before parallelizing: cProfile, or py-spy to see the real bottleneck (and GIL contention with --gil)
It doesn't help when tasks are tiny (pickling and scheduling cost more than the work itself)
It doesn't help when a shared bottleneck (DB pool, API rate limit, a single disk, memory bandwidth) is already saturated
Too much concurrency hurts: more threads than needed cause contention and memory blow-up, and unbounded asyncio fan-out causes server-side 429s
uvloop can speed up the asyncio loop's I/O dispatch, but it won't fix blocking calls or CPU-bound coroutines

chapters.title: Cheatsheet: Python Concurrency at a Glance
points: Decision table: I/O plus async libraries → asyncio; I/O plus blocking libraries → threads; CPU → processes, or free-threaded threads
Threads: ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers).map(fn, items). Cheap to share memory, limited by the GIL for CPU work
Processes: ProcessPoolExecutor with the __main__ guard, picklable args, and chunksize for many small tasks
asyncio: asyncio.run(main()), with TaskGroup for fan-out, timeout() for deadlines and Semaphore for limits
trio/anyio: nurseries and task groups, move_on_after/fail_after, ExceptionGroup handled with except*
Bridges: to_thread / run_in_executor (sync from async), run_coroutine_threadsafe / call_soon_threadsafe (async from a thread)
Free-threaded: python3.13t or 3.14t, check sys._is_gil_enabled(), audit C-extension support
Safety: Lock for read-modify-write, Queue for handoff, ContextVar for per-task state, and never block the event loop
Before scaling out: profile, measure with perf_counter or pyperf, apply Amdahl's law, check the shared bottleneck
Red flags: time.sleep in async def, lost task references, swallowed CancelledError, fork with threads, Manager in hot loops
